extracted.intended_audience: historians of technology, inventors/engineers interested in historical practices of invention and patenting
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria concern how early-19th-century inventors (Stephenson et al.) discovered, tested, documented, and sought recognition/patenting for mechanical inventions (safety-lamp, locomotive), including experimental, design, documentary, and priority-evidence practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental verification of the core principle
rubrics_metrics.description: 'By experiment he distinctly ascertained that the explosion of fire-damp could not pass through small tubes' (i.e. demonstrate the central physical fact underpinning the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform direct experiments to establish the fundamental fact or principle on which the invention rests; the book stresses establishing 'the fact' even if the theoretical rationale is not yet known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and test a working prototype in real conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson 'constructed a lamp on such a principle, and repeatedly proved its safety at the risk of his life' — construct actual devices and prove their function and safety in the intended environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prototype must be operated in situ (e.g., in foul air/blowers in mines) and shown by repeated trials to perform the intended safety/function; demonstrations to practical users strengthen the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative experiments to determine operating parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'made the mixtures in all proportions... found by the experiments that when a current... forced up a tube 4/10 of an inch in diameter, the necessary current was 9 inches in a second to prevent its coming down that tube.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and record quantitative thresholds (diameter, velocity, mixture proportions) that define safe/working limits — use instruments, timed/measured trials, and numerical data to substantiate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat trials and record observations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'These experiments were repeated several times' and trials were 'repeated in various ways' — repetition to verify consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform multiple repetitions and variations of the experiment; use assistants/observers and record data (e.g., pendulum vibrations) to document repeatability and robustness; note and learn from failures ('two or three blows up').

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative design improvement driven by experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson altered slides, added more tubes, proposed surrounding oil vessel with capillary tubes, cut off middles, made holes in metal plates — successive modifications based on observed issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experimental feedback to iteratively modify design (alter apertures, tube counts/diameters, arrangement of openings) until desired performance is achieved; document design changes and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for failure modes and stress conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments 'were not performed without risk' and they experienced 'blows up' when flame descended into the receiver; Davy lamp tests sometimes become 'decidedly unsafe' under current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately test under adverse/high-stress conditions to reveal failure modes (strong currents, explosive mixtures); observe behavior (extinguishing vs red-hot gauze) and compare designs for worst-case safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-testing and public demonstration to relevant stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson tested lamps at Killin gworth pit, 'produced several bladders full of carburetted hydrogen' and 'proved the safety of his lamp by numerous experiments' before the Philosophical and Literary Society and local miners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the invention before affected users (miners), local societies, or public bodies to show practical utility and gain recognition; include demonstrable experiments during presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare written specification and obtain a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This improved form of rail and chair was embodied in a patent... the specification of the same patent also described various important improvements in the locomotive itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a clear specification describing construction and claimed improvements (rails, chairs, locomotive features) and pursue formal patent protection; include practical details sufficient for reproduction and legal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain dated records, witnesses, and testimonials to support priority claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson's dates of first/second/third lamp trials (21 Oct, 4 Nov, 30 Nov 1815), committee testimony (1835), public letters, and subscriptions/testimonials were used in the controversy over priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep dated experimental records, witness statements, and public demonstrations; deposit or publish contemporaneous accounts (letters, society presentations) to establish precedence in priority disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical efficacy can trump theoretical understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Stephenson's theory ... was no doubt wrong; but his lamp was right' — a working invention need not have a correct scientific theory to be meritorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let incomplete theoretical explanation prevent patenting or promotion if the device demonstrably works; emphasize empirical proof of function when theory is unsettled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with skilled craftsmen and financiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson took the lamp to a tinman, a plumber drew the design, Mr. Losh (iron-founder) financed the patent taken out in joint names, and workmen produced the lamps quickly from rough sketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partner with skilled manufacturers and patrons to realize a design and to fund patenting/manufacture; practical fabrication skills and capital are essential to move from idea to patented product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design infrastructure and system-level considerations alongside device design
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson regarded the road and the locomotive as 'one machine' and emphasized road perfection (solidity, continuity, smoothness) as crucial to locomotive success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the supporting infrastructure (rails, chairs, road alignment) when designing an invention that operates in a system — improvements may be required in the environment to realize full benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve joints and supports to reduce jolts and wear
rubrics_metrics.description: He adopted the 'half-lap joint' instead of the butt-joint, made chairs with curved apex bottoms, and extended supports spacing to reduce jolts and fractures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rail joints and seating/chairs to ensure level continuity and distribute loads smoothly; use overlapping joints/scarf-like ends and appropriate chair geometry to minimize impact and wear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate materials for durability and weight savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Wheels were altered 'from cast to malleable iron' making them lighter, more durable and safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose materials that reduce weight while improving durability and safety; material selection can materially affect performance and lifespan of mechanical components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovate mechanical substitutes when standard components unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of suitable springs he arranged the boiler supported by four cylinders with pistons acting as springs to equalize weight and soften jerks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When standard components (e.g., strong springs) are not available, devise alternative mechanisms (steam-supported floating pistons) to achieve required functions like load equalization and shock absorption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure performance quantitatively with custom instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson used a dynamometer of his own construction to test resistance to traction and ascertained friction was constant at all velocities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build or adapt instruments to measure relevant performance metrics (resistance, friction, rolling resistance); quantitative measurement should drive design and operational decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and quantify the main sources of resistance affecting performance
rubrics_metrics.description: He ascertained resistances were mainly: axle friction, rolling resistance between wheel and rail, and gravity; rolling resistance varied with roughness and could be dominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down total resistance into components, quantify each, and address the most significant contributors (e.g., smooth rail surfaces to reduce rolling resistance) to improve efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess economic feasibility based on empirical data
rubrics_metrics.description: From experiments he concluded steam carriages on common roads were uneconomical due to high rolling resistance; small gradients (1 in 100) greatly reduced useful effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experimental measurements to evaluate whether an invention is economically viable in its intended application; factor in gradients, surface roughness, and operational costs before broad deployment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan alignment and civil works to optimize operational performance
rubrics_metrics.description: He argued in favour of perforating hills with long tunnels and raising lower levels (cut-and-fill) so railways could be as nearly level as possible for economical operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an invention's performance depends on route geometry (e.g., locomotives), plan and invest in civil works (tunnels, cut/fill) to achieve optimal grades that minimize energy losses and operational penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge prior observations and distinguish independent application
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes Tennant and Wollaston had observed the fact earlier; both Stephenson and Davy may have been independent, and priority claims were disputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research prior art and publicly known observations; document how your contribution differs (application, construction, testing) from prior knowledge to support novelty and independent invention claims.
